newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Routed Thai stocks set for uneasy breather.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Routed Thai stocks set for uneasy breather.

text.p: Chart in hand, it would be easy for a technical analyst to argue that Thailand's battered stock market is ready for a healthy rebound.

The benchmark SET index has lost a third of its value since the end of last year and is languishing at around 560, territory unvisited since the days when Thailand's economic miracle was being declared eight years ago.

But few investors are in a mood for charts, with forecasts for economic growth constantly being pared back, export growth lacklustre, currency headaches, a financial sector crisis and the prospect of a budget gap for the first time in a decade.
"Markets overshoot all the time," said one analyst at a European brokerage.
"They overshoot on the upside and they overshoot on the downside. Right now no one here wants to buy because they know in their own minds that it's going lower."
He was echoing what many believe -- that, despite declining interest rates and a 50-billion-baht ($1.9-billion) support fund waiting in the wings, this market is not about to turn around.
None of those contacted by Reuters saw the SET making a convincing challenge on the 600 in the near term. And, none would rule out a swoop below this year's low of 544.10.

Nimit Wongjariakul, senior vice president at Thaimex Finance and Securities, said investors were still reeling from last week's news that a merger which many hoped would rescue the cash-strapped Finance One company had fallen through.
"I think short term we may see a really strong impact on the SET," he said. "After that people will get numb with it for a while and then, hopefully, it will stabilise."
Trading system glitches left traders just 33 minutes to deal on Monday, but the SET still ended down 2.2 percent. Since then, business has slowed to a trickle and volatility has dropped.

"There could be a bit of a consolidation. People are wondering if the market is at its bottom and it's time to buy," said Supaval Saicheua, Vice President of the finance and securities firm Krungthai Thanakit Public.

He said the market remained vulnerable to bad news such as another wobble on the baht after the recent attack by speculators, or the collapse of one of the country's many cash-strapped and heavily indebted financial companies.
In the short term, investors will look to Thursday's trade data for a pointer on an economy whose growth the government now expects to be 5.9 percent this year after 6.7 percent in 1996.
Longer term, they are likely to look coolly at signs that corporate earnings are on a downswing.
Blue chip Siam Cement was the latest to add to that picture, announcing on Wednesday that its first-quarter net profit had dropped 30 percent to 1.91 billion baht ($74 million).
Analysts said that while the bourse has dropped like a stone, the overall price/earnings ratio has not fallen so far because of the lean times that so many companies are facing.
Supaval said the market's overall p/e ratio may now have slipped below 10 compared with 11-12 earlier in the year.
